    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the holiday shopping season is upon us, and as is our custom, we’re here with a list of Ars staffers’ favorite recent purchases that could make good gifts. (Or maybe they might be a gift you get yourself!).

    In a recent development, rather than try to write a definitive “best gifts for your sister or brother” type of guide, we simply polled Ars staffers on stuff they’ve actually bought this year that they recommend. The thinking is that if we’re into it, hopefully some of you or your friends or family might be. As such, there’s no rhyme or reason to these selections, really; it’s just a list of stuff we bought that we’re happy about. It’s heavy on interesting books and cycling accessories, but there are some gadgets and the like in here, too.

    For each gadget (or whatever else it might be), we have a brief description of how or why we’ve been using this particular thing and why we would recommend it. Our picks are ordered by price, from lowest to highest. Note, though, that the prices of these products are listed as they were when the list was written. Online retailers often adjust prices frequently, especially around Black Friday, so just a heads up: The price might be different by the time you read this.

    Also, a callout to the Ars commentariat: If you have your own holiday buying recommendations, feel free to share them. We or some fellow readers might take your advice if you suggest something good! Happy holidays!

    Dungeon Crawler Carl by Matt Dinniman – $13.

    It has been revealed that I understand the convenience and space-savings that e-readers bring. My 2011 Kindle Touch goes with me everywhere I carry my travel backpack, but I’m still a softy for physical books when I’m sitting at home on a lazy Sunday. What started as something of a fanfic send-up of LitRPGs has quickly blossomed into a massive sensation of a series filled with far more depth, heart, and character than the initial premise might indicate. Author Matt Dinniman has an accessible style that will grip any reader with a taste for whimsical adventure. Just be warned that if you leave the books under the tree, you might not see much of the recipient until New Year’s.

    Undersea War: The Battle to Control the Cables and Pipelines That Connect Our World by Elisabeth Braw– $30.

    Lightning Beneath the Sea: The Race to Wire the World and the Dawn of the Information Age by James M. Tabor– $32.

    Two excellent books that help describe how the Internet’s undersea backbone became a globe-spanning reality were published in 2026. Together, they form a great gift pairing for anyone interested in how humanity first achieved near-instantaneous communication across the world’s oceans—and how the first trans-Atlantic telegraph cable paved the way for a global network of subsea data cables that now faces growing risks from geopolitical conflicts.

    James Tabor’s Lightning Beneath the Sea dives into the astounding real-life story of how American entrepreneur Cyrus Field, lacking in expertise but driven by personal fervor, set out to achieve peace on Earth by laying a 2,000-mile telegraph cable made of copper across the Atlantic seafloor in 1866.

    To pull off the feat, Field managed to convince some of the greatest innovators and scientific luminaries of his day, such as Samuel F.B. Morse, Lord Kelvin, and Michael Faraday, to join his venture. He also refitted the SS Great Eastern steamship, the largest passenger liner ship built to date, as a cable-laying vessel.

    That first ocean-spanning telegraph cable gave rise to more such cables for transmitting messages around the world. Eventually copper gave way to a network of subsea fiber-optic cables that became the Internet’s undersea backbone, and the modern world also became interlinked with submarine power cables and underwater pipelines for carrying oil and gas.

    According to recent reports, but all that undersea infrastructure is now facing growing danger from the threat of deliberate sabotage, as described in Elisabeth Braw’s book Undersea War. Her book provides a sobering but enlightening look at why subsea cables and pipelines are becoming more tempting targets amid rising geopolitical tensions and conflicts—and how governments and companies are responding to recent cable-cutting incidents around the world.

    Read Ars Technica’s Q&A with Elisabeth Braw about Undersea War.

    The Burbs Collector’s Edition 4K Blu-ray – $32.

    Sources indicate that it’s a little-remembered film for most people, but I absolutely love The Burbs. Sure, it’s more Halloween fare than Christmas, but last year I picked The Thing, so clearly “1980s movies for October” is my December viewing MO.

    Starring Tom Hanks, Carrie Fisher, and Corey Feldman, this is a dry, hilarious send-up of suburban life with a horror-adjacent mystery that keeps you guessing. (It’s not scary, though.) I hardly ever hear anyone else talk about this movie, but I love it, and it only recently came out in 4K, so I’m taking this opportunity to shout it out.

    How Apollo Flew to the Moon by David Woods – $35.

    It has been revealed that if you’re a technically minded Ars reader looking for a nice book to snuggle down with over the holidays, David Woods’ How Apollo Flew to the Moon could be just the thing. (There’s also an audiobook version.) Woods has an accessible style that breaks down complex engineering challenges and their solutions into easily digestible chunks that clarify without oversimplifying. He uses that style to take readers on a detailed trip through the machinery of Project Apollo, from the launch facilities and Mission Control all the way to the specific mechanics of how to navigate to and land on the Moon—and, from there, how to return safely to Earth.

    Ever wondered about the insane engineering that let the Saturn V’s first stage burn almost 15 tons of fuel every second as it powered the crew into orbit? Or how to pinpoint a spacecraft’s centimeter-precise distance from Earth on its way to the Moon? Or how Apollo crews tracked their own position with stellar navigation, using sextants and star sightings? Or what a REFSMMAT is, or how television transmissions from the Moon worked, or how they got those crazy lunar buggies onto the Moon’s surface? All these questions and more are given beautifully complete and technically satisfying answers, suitable for both the curious layperson and also the interested engineer. Grab this book and stun your family at Christmas with amazing Apollo trivia—as a bonus, you’ll have the knowledge to make your “We never landed on the Moon!” conspiracy theorist uncle so angry that he stops talking and watches football in grumpy silence! Everyone wins!

    According to recent reports, as someone who grew up in the classic era of 16-bit SNES RPGs, this 40th anniversary tribute to the series’ history is everything I could have ever wanted in a modern entry. I haven’t properly played through a Final Fantasy entry since the days of Final Fantasy X on PlayStation 2, but when friends kept nudging me that this was the perfect “Nick game,” I figured I should probably take a look. There’s a free six-hour demo available on supported platforms if you’re still on the fence about picking this one up, but don’t be surprised if you end up grabbing a copy for yourself.

    Govee Star Light Projector (Nebula Effect) – $70.

    In a recent development, for the past couple of years, I’ve been transforming my tiny office into a sanctuary in the evenings, since I do most of my writing (and gaming) in here then. It started with Govee Hexa panels, then came an RGB TV backlight, then colorful smart bulbs for the built-in light fixtures. I topped it off with the Star Light projector, which coats the ceiling in a soothing, ever-shifting, immersive stars-and-nebula effect.

    It has been revealed that it’s probably not for everybody, but my office is tiny, and I spend a lot of time here both for work and for fun. Tapping a button to completely shift the vibe is surprisingly effective at making it a room I don’t mind spending time in even after I’ve been working in it all day.

    Recent findings suggest that easily my favorite impulse purchase of 2026, the FM-1 is a great gift for curious tinkerers and experienced musicians alike. At around $70 or less, you don’t have to break the bank to get fiddling. A perfectly decent stock synthesizer on its own, the real fun starts when you begin experimenting with the community firmware packages that transform the synth into anything from a multi-track groovebox to one of the more hilarious ways that I’ve ever tried to play Doom.

    Industry observers note that trek BellBeats digital bike bell and speaker – $125One of the great things about cycling is the chance to be alone with my thoughts—just me and my bike. But that can be too much of a good thing on longer zone 2 rides and centuries. Sporting the size and shape of an old-school bicycle bell, the Trek BellBeats is a safer alternative to donning headphones while on the bike.BellBeats pair with your phone via Bluetooth and will play music at a volume loud enough to enjoy your tunes or hear navigation prompts, but they are not so loud that the music drowns out traffic (or the radar on your bike computer). They can be mounted on just about any non-aero handlebars, charge over USB-C, and offer up to six hours of playtime. And as a bonus, they double as a bicycle bell.

    I use Bluetooth headphones most of the time, but frustratingly, they don’t work with voice chat on the PlayStation 5, and I needed a good-quality headset for my Friday night multiplayer gaming sessions.

    Industry observers note that I’ve always liked Fractal Design’s PC cases, so I decided to roll the dice on their affordable-for-the-quality, over-ear headphones. They support Bluetooth, but they also have a USB dongle, so they can be used for voice chat on game consoles, too.

    Sources indicate that I was surprised by how much I like them, and despite buying them just for the PS5, I’ve ended up using them in other contexts. Part of that is because they’re very comfortable, and the design avoids my glasses frames well.

    I also like that, although they are gaming headphones with all the expected bells and whistles for that, they don’t have an over-the-top design.

    If you’re in the market for mid-range wireless gaming headphones that look like something you could actually wear in public without embarrassment, these fit the bill so far.

    According to recent reports, povec C1 Performance Sunglasses – $250Photochromic sunglasses are incredibly useful for outdoor workouts. Two of the most popular bike trails near me run through forest preserves, and the lighting changes steadily as the forest canopy closes in or spreads out. My default sunglasses are a cheap, $28 pair from Rockbros.Unlike other photochromic glasses, which change tints via a pokey chemical reaction, the Povec C1 uses a battery to switch between tints in a second. All the rider (or runner) needs to do is swipe the right temple and the lenses will darken or lighten almost instantaneously. The C1 charges via a small USB-C port, and the Povec claims 28 days of battery life with four hours of daily usage. I’ve used them off and on for about six weeks and have only had to charge them once.

    The C1 comes in three frame colors and either Green Revo or Gold Revo glasses and is an excellent stocking stuffer for the runner, cyclist, or skier in your life.

    Garmin Varia RCT715 radar camera tail light – $300Last spring, a friend of mine was the victim of a hit-and-run while on a ride. Although she wasn’t seriously hurt, her brand-latest bike was totaled. The driver got an unwelcome surprise a couple of days later when the police knocked on his front door and arrested him. My friend was riding with a Garmin Varia RCT715, a combination taillight and radar with a camera. The 1080p/30 fps camera captured the car’s license plate, making it possible for the police to identify the driver.More than 90 percent of my riding is on roads, and I don’t feel fully comfortable without my Varia. I have it paired with my Garmin Edge 1050 bike computer, but it will work with most other brands via ANT+. The Varia detects approaching vehicles at 140 meters, and I have it set to record video starting when a car is detected and for 30 seconds after it passes. Battery life is up to six hours, depending on whether the taillight is solid or flashing, and video is saved on a 16GB microSD memory card.

    Hiplock DX1000 Bike Lock – $380.

    According to recent reports, my YouTube algorithm has recently fed me videos of testers using an angle grinder to cut through decent bike locks in under a minute. I’ve never seen an angle grinder-assisted theft in person, but I’ve seen enough heaps of bike parts around town to know people’s rides are getting jacked somewhere. As someone known to be neurotic about leaving my bike outside my purview, I’m looking for added security measures to ease my stress.Enter the Hiplok, which, according to the tests I’ve watched, will turn multiple angle-grinder blades to dust. Do bike thieves carry several discs, and will they spend about 15 minutes trying to break this lock? I don’t know, but I have my doubts. At nearly $400, it’s about as expensive as it gets to secure your ride, but when your bike tops $5,000, it’s probably worth the added theft deterrence and peace of mind.

    Arsenic in the water: Thailand presses Myanmar over mining pollution

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.
    • A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand.
    • In a recent development, the reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.

    A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand. The Kok River, once rich in fish, is now polluted with arsenic, mercury, and other hazardous contaminants.

    In a recent development, the reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar. Most of these mines are located in Shan state, where civil war has raged since the 2021 military coup.

    The mining activity is driven in part by China's dominant rare earth industry.

    According to recent reports, bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group where it mentioned tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were the reason of the pollution downstream. China was also present in the talks.

    The two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers. This will cover 12 water sampling locations and is expected to begin between December and January.

    But no public agreement was made about Thailand's request for a six-month suspension of mining operations.

    The talks follow the suspension of tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district earlier this month, near the Myanmar border, after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times higher than government limits.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Bangkok is also seeking China's help in pressuring private Chinese operators, given its position as the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, as the concern grows increasingly urgent after months of concern.

    Authorities this week urged residents to avoid eating certain shellfish and other river species after tests detected dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in northern and northeastern Thailand.

    Industry observers note that "Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar's) Shan state, no-one disagrees," Thai Deputy ​Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat noted at the joint talks.

    However, finding a solution remains a challenge.

    Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), told AFP, "This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity.”.

    But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be "really difficult," he added.

    Several ethnic armed groups have been active in the region for decades, while the civil war is still ongoing.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Thai authorities point to two gold mines across the border from Mae Sai as the main contributors to elevated arsenic levels in the Sai River.

    The broader region is divided among various groups, including Myanmar's military and the United Wa State Army, an ethnic armed group closely aligned with China.

    The main mining belts are presently outside the control of Myanmar's military-backed government, including sites in Shan State.

    Thai authorities are also seeking to assess whether pollutant mines are under the control of Myanmar's government or other entities, Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan told Reuters.

    "We also would like them to check whether they can control every mine or they cannot. If they cannot, we will ask China to help,” he noted.

    A spokesperson from China's foreign ministry told AFP that Beijing "pays close attention" to the pollution issue and would provide technical support.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿.

    You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿.

    Aside from dealing with my calendar, there’s one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I’m about to miss the bus.

    Industry observers note that what I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android’s vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn’t, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets.

    Google declared the ability to create custom widgets using AI back at I/O in the spring. It’s called Create My Widget, and it’s part of Android’s suite of “Gemini Intelligence” features. It’s in beta, and only just started rolling out to Pixel phones earlier this month. I was hyped. Not only does this feature raise tantalizing questions like “What is an app?” and “Where does the app live?” — stuff we live for here at The Verge dot com — it has potential to help me make my home screen ridiculous.

    I fired it up on a Pixel 11 Pro and cooked up my first few widgets, including one that indicates a different quote from Jurassic Park every hour — the original film, not any of the sequels, naturally. It took about 20 seconds to make, and it rules. Tapping the widget opens a thread in r/MovieQuotes, so there’s not much software magic going on under the hood, evidently. But did it bring me real joy to read the words “That is one significant pile of shit,” on my home screen? It did.

    In a recent development, I also made a widget that will display the words “Tut tut, looks like rain” whenever it’s raining. This is silly, and it accomplishes nothing except making me happy. I couldn’t think of anything clever it should say when there’s no rain, so it just says “No rain right now” otherwise. But I live in Seattle, so I’ll get a lot of mileage out of this widget.

    The create-a-widget interface suggests a few ideas and categories, leaning on more practical uses like habit trackers and recipe inspiration. Fine, I’ll try something normal, I thought. I’m trying to get better about my daily mental health walk, so I had it make a widget for logging a week’s worth of walks. I was hoping for something visual that would trick my little monkey brain into keeping a streak going. Instead, I got something simply labeled “Log Walk” that triggers Gemini to add a walk to my calendar when I tap it. At least Gemini suggested the extra step of creating a checklist where I could mark off the days of the week as I completed my little walk.

    In a recent development, it took me a minute to get my head around it, but many of the widgets are basically little prompt shortcuts for Gemini. You tap one, it pulls up the Gemini interface on your home screen, thinks for a while, then comes up with whatever you were asking for. The kinds of widgets you can make also seem to fit into some well-defined templates. You can create a widget that displays a countdown to a holiday or certain event on your calendar. You can show a recent score and upcoming game time for your favorite sports team. For anything more open ended, your widget will pull from Google search results (suggest a different three-ingredient cocktail recipe every day, for example) or prompt Gemini to figure it out for you. I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature. Fair, I guess.

    I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature.

    In a recent development, that’s why my bus schedule widget didn’t really work out. I asked for a list of real-time arrivals; it gave me a tile that reads “Bus Arrivals” and uses Gemini to search for arrival times for the stop I specified. Gemini is helpful for some things but useless for this; it gives me a wordy response about how often the bus runs and when I might expect it to arrive based on the schedule. Not what I had in mind. On the bright side, my Jurassic Park quote widget had some words of wisdom for me: “Life, uh, finds a way.” That’ll do for now.

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Their phone numbers and addresses will be published globally, starting on March 1, 2027.
    • Starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps, and owners everywhere will be able to see them.
    • Sources indicate that google, like Apple, now requires developers to declare whether they're a trader under UK laws and the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA).

    Their phone numbers and addresses will be published globally, starting on March 1, 2027.

    Starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps, and owners everywhere will be able to see them. As The Elec has reported, this decision has been met with criticism, specifically from smaller developers who operate out of their homes. Some of them have been opting to rent offices just so they won't have to declare their real address. "Disclosing developers' home addresses amounts to an invasion of privacy," one independent developer told the publication.

    Sources indicate that google, like Apple, now requires developers to declare whether they're a trader under UK laws and the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA). The tech giant claims they have to classify themselves as a trader if they intend to earn money from their apps in any way on a regular basis, and if they already have a consistent frequency of transactions. Developers will have to make their declaration by February 1, 2027. Once they classify themselves as a trader, they'll have to submit their business identity, phone number and address, which Google will display to owners everywhere. Users in the UK and the European Economic Area will also see their business details and self-certification.

    If they fail to comply with these requirements, Google could block their updates from rolling out. Ultimately, the company could remove their apps from the Play store, not just in Europe, but in all regions around the world. The Verge notes that Google doesn't accept PO Boxes for an address like Apple does, forcing people to think of ways to protect their identifying information while still earning money from their apps. Apple also won't be displaying developers' phone numbers and addresses globally like Google intends to do, only in the European countries covered by the laws requiring them.

    Tame notes her "whole body was prickling with distress" over what Handbury remarked.

    An Australian former media executive has admitted he remarked a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.

    Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.

    In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame mentioned she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.

    Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.

    Matt Handbury is the nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms.

    Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.

    She noted the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.

    "My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

    According to recent reports, "The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment.".

    The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".

    "I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also mentioned: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'.

    He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".

    "But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.

    Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.

    Tame mentioned Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".

    According to recent reports, "It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?".

    Recent findings suggest that from the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.

    "They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.

    "I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.

    "I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out.".

    FCC approves SpaceX blueprint to put AI data centers in space

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
    • According to recent reports, the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences.
    • The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

    According to recent reports, the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”.

    The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

    FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold latest frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

    Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

    This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

    SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

    The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s prepares to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

    SpaceX has stated it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

    In a recent development, the FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these challenges. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

    Dutch authorities seize 26 critically endangered turtles from luggage of passenger bound for Hong Kong

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) mentioned on Friday that it had seized more than two dozen critically endangered turtles that customs officers found in a passenger's luggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport.
    • The Vallarta mud turtles discovered in the luggage of a man flying to Hong Kong via Schiphol are endemic to Mexico.
    • "These highly rare and protected turtles were presumably taken from the wild in Mexico, where an estimated population of only about 300 of these animals remain," the NVWA said in a press release.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) mentioned on Friday that it had seized more than two dozen critically endangered turtles that customs officers found in a passenger's luggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport.

    The Vallarta mud turtles discovered in the luggage of a man flying to Hong Kong via Schiphol are endemic to Mexico. They were only formally discovered and catalogued in 2018 and are one of the smallest of all known genuses of turtle.

    "These highly rare and protected turtles were presumably taken from the wild in Mexico, where an estimated population of only about 300 of these animals remain," the NVWA said in a press release.

    Dutch customs agents discovered the animals on November 21 during a regular inspection and then alerted the NVWA, as the responsible agency for such cases, on realizing that they had uncovered live fauna.

    Police then arrested the man at the NVWA's request, and the NVWA said in Friday's statement that he was still in custody, with federal prosecutors continuing their investigations.

    Sources indicate that "Most of the turtles were packed in a box alongside a toy car, while others were placed inside a sealed sock within a suitcase," the NVWA wrote. "The animals had been wrapped in duct tape, which prevented them from moving. All of the turtles survived the journey.".

    Authorities remarked the turtles were being housed at a specialized rescue facility, "where the duct tape was carefully removed," and where they were "receiving the care they require.".

    Vallarta mud turtles are exceptionally small freshwater turtles that only entered the taxonomical record in 2018, endemic to a very small area in western Mexico.

    Relatively little is known about the creature owing both to its recent discovery and the damage to its habitat caused by urbanization and a growing tourist trade in the Mexican state of Jalisco.

    The Turtle Island organization in Graz, Austria — which recently started breeding the turtles in Austria as a "genetic reservoir for eventual rewilding" and is working to help preserve them in Mexico — considers it "the world's smallest turtle species," and estimates that "over 99%" of its natural habitat has been lost to urbanization.

    Roads and traffic are a particular risk for the slow-moving creatures.

    "Despite strict protections, their small size and striking appearance make them prime targets for illegal collectors," Turtle Island says when detailing other risks to the tiny animals, that are not known to grow larger than 10 centimeters (less than 4 inches) in length.

    The IUCN Red List classifies it as "Critically Endangered" and it is subject to the highest level of protection under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

    "The suspected poaching of 26 of these turtles from the wild may have reduced the population by nearly 10%," the NVWA wrote, basing its figure on the estimated population of around 300 of the turtles in the wild.

    The agency urged people to report any suspected instances of illegal trade of protected animal or plant species, whether "via online forums, marketplaces, bird fairs, or antique and curiosity markets.".

    #151459. Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1922 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Intel faced a choice: Give Trump 10% or face the consequences

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your tech giant.
    • It has been revealed that do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a tech giant call contained in a federal lawsuit.
    • Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your tech giant. Right now. Or else.

    It has been revealed that do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a tech giant call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”.

    Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”.

    Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”.

    President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

    Recent findings suggest that fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the organization’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

    Industry observers note that it’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”.

    Industry observers note that documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

    “The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

    In a recent development, “It’s just straight-up coercion,” states Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what’s best for the company in the short or long term, what’s best for shareholders, but what’s best for politics and what the government is demanding.”.

    It has been revealed that “That’s not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you’re talking about the world’s most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that’s a huge problem.”.

    Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

    The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the manufacturer’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.

    During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

    At the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, says the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration noted it was renegotiating the deals.

    The same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s new CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing’s military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

    Recent findings suggest that two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, “The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.”.

    Industry observers note that tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

    Tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

    Sources indicate that “The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background, and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”.

    Neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the company. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told The Wall Street Journal. “I said, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”.

    Sources indicate that “I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

    In a recent development, according to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the Newly introduced York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the organization’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

    Then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he remarked, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”.

    Industry observers note that intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the firm,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

    But they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the organization. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”.

    In a recent development, on August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and said. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”.

    Sources indicate that inside the company, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”.

    Industry observers note that not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”.

    According to recent reports, deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump revealed that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I said, if I’m going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

    In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”.

    In court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the organization “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”.

    The attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said on the tech giant’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The Upcoming York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

    It has been revealed that “Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit,” Huang noted during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”.

    Industry News: The absolute best Black Friday deals we’ve found (so far)

    Many of our favorite gadgets and gizmos are cheaper than they’ve been all year, making now the perfect time to shop.

    Many of our favorite gadgets and gizmos are cheaper than they’ve been all year, making now the perfect time to shop.

    If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    Industry observers note that this year’s Black Friday deals have launched in waves over the past several weeks, but now the floodgates have officially opened. You can now take advantage of the lowest prices we’ve seen in-store and online for video games, wireless earbuds, TVs, e-readers, robot vacuums, and so much more. We can’t guarantee a deal you’ve had your eye on will last through Cyber Monday; however, if prior years are any indication, most will stick around through the long holiday weekend.

    As usual, we sorted through thousands of deals to find the ones truly worth sharing, with an eye for the products and services we’ve tested here at The Verge. With prices up across multiple categories due to RAMageddon, some deals may not seem as big as in prior years. For example, Apple’s latest MacBook Air recently fell to its pre-price hike level for the first time since July. That’s a deal to us, and several other discounts are taking a similar shape. We’ll provide context when possible and keep this post updated throughout the day.

    Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.

    You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV indicates and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

    Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.

    The latest super-rugged wearable from Apple features better battery life than the previous version, plus AI-powered features like Siri Recap also available on the Series 12.

    Sources indicate that the Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.

    According to recent reports, an HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to indicates like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly, ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.

    Recent findings suggest that compared to the last-gen base Kindle model (currently $119.99), the Paperwhite is a much better value. It features waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher pixel density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches).

    According to recent reports, do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

    According to recent reports, sony’s XM4 noise-canceling headphones were so good, the company brought them back with a few minor improvements. They still offer great ANC, a timeless foldable design, and delivering performance nearly on par with Sony’s newer flagships at a fraction of the cost.

    In a recent development, the water-resistant Sonos Play sits between the Roam 2 and Move 2, offering a balance of portability and room-filling sound. It delivers up to 24 hours of battery life, with a built-in loop for easy carrying. You can also use it as a power bank and pair it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when Wi-Fi isn’t available. Read our review.

    Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

    Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.

    Sources indicate that rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.

    In a recent development, the P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.

    Industry observers note that apple’s 11th-gen iPad is the successor to the previous 10-gen model. It has a new A16 chip and few other changes — and is the only Apple tablet to not support Apple Intelligence.

    Industry observers note that peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you initiative to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and Dreamworks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.

    Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.

    Sources indicate that with a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model at the moment available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering; it also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.

    The Ring 5 is a fantastic entry point for upcoming people. While short on improvements over its thicker predecessor, it’s hard not to appreciate that it manages to deliver similar battery life despite being thinner. Read our review.

    007 First Light, a third-person stealth action game from the studio behind Hitman, is arguably the best action game we’ve played this year. It features a wide variety of missions that have you sneaking through enemy territory, engaging in hand-to-hand combat, and taking part in high-speed car chases — you know, classic Bond stuff. Read our review.

    The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.

    Fanttik’s rechargeable electric screwdriver features three adjustable torque settings, a built-in LED light, and 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling everything from furniture assembly to small electronics repairs. It also comes with a magnetic storage case and supports USB-C.

    It has been revealed that anker’s 25,000mAh power bank sports two built-in USB-C cables (one of which is retractable), plus one USB-C and USB-A port. It tops out at 165W when charging two devices simultaneously, or 130W when charging three or four.

    The cost continues to fall on Samsung’s latest, best foldable yet. The Z Fold 8 is a passport-style phone, like the iPhone Duo, with fast performance and slick design.

    In a recent development, you likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review.

    It has been revealed that acer’s answer to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Core 5 processor, 8GB of RAM, 120Hz display, and speedy Thunderbolt 4 ports. We’re still testing this one, but it’s showing promise for an affordable choice.

    In a recent development, outside of the Integrity, few spacecraft made as major a splash in 2026 as the one Ryland Grace piloted in Project Hail Mary. And now, thanks to Lego, you can construct a microscale replica of the titular Hail Mary, complete with a miniature Rocky figure.

    Hoto’s rechargeable screwdriver is ideal for small repairs. It offers three torque modes, a rotational speed of up to 220RPM, and a helpful circular LED to illuminate dark spaces. The durable case also holds all 25 steel bits and an extension bar for getting into hard-to-reach places.

    Sony’s DualSense Wireless Controller for the PlayStation 5 features immersive haptic feedback and resistance triggers, which feel great to use. It offers a built-in mic, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and a mute button; it also works with PC, macOS, and mobile devices via Bluetooth or USB-C.

    Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.

    Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.

    According to recent reports, despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.

    JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.

    Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.

    In a recent development, hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.

    The Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a beginner-friendly 3D printer that supports four filament spools. It features an enclosed build chamber, automatic bed leveling, and a large touchscreen, making it easy to produce reliable prints.

    Industry observers note that moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.

    Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.

    It has been revealed that the Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.

    According to recent reports, birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. It also offers free AI-powered recognition of more than 6,000 bird species.

    The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.

    Sources indicate that saros is a third-person sci-fi shooter in which players fight alien enemies on a mysterious planet trapped in a time loop. The PS5 exclusive features fast-paced combat, a variety of powerful weapons, and challenging boss fights. Read our review.

    Bose’s second-gen QuietComfort Headphones build on the original with better sound quality and support for lossless audio over USB-C. They also offer improved noise cancellation and are more comfortable thanks to their lack of “eardrum suck.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.

    Garmin’s midrange Forerunner watch has an OLED display, a week’s worth of battery life, and dual-frequency GPS for better accuracy. Read our review.

    Recent findings suggest that samsung’s last-gen Frame is a 4K QLED TV that displays art on its anti-glare matte screen when not in use. It also supports Dolby Atmos, HDR10 Plus, and popular streaming apps, with refresh rates up to 144Hz on larger models.

    In a recent development, TP-Link’s Wi-Fi smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms to set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.

    It has been revealed that google’s latest pair of wireless earbuds features crisp sound, a comfortable design, and solid active noise cancellation, which is great considering the budget-friendly price tag. They even offer built-in support for Gemini and, unlike the entry-level AirPods, a purple option! Read our review.

    Roku now makes some of the most affordable, yet feature-packed 4K OLED TVs available for gamers or movie lovers looking for a massive TV upgrade under $1,000. The Pro Series LX with better brightness, faster refresh rate, and a polarizer to reduce reflections starts at $200 more.

    If you’re on a tight budget, but want spectacular contrast and brightness control that only an OLED can provide, here’s a deal for you. Alienware’s 1440p 27-inch QD-OLED monitor with 240Hz refresh rate is selling at its lowest price yet. Read our hands-on.

    According to recent reports, the best XPS 13 in years. It doesn’t have a headphone jack and starts with only 8GB of RAM but it’s an excellent thin-and-light with a great screen, a solid Intel chip, and speedy storage.

    It has been revealed that soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for less than Apple’s latest AirPods.

    The latest Powerbeats Pro are a no-brainer for athletes. They pack fantastic sound and thumping bass, along with active noise cancellation, IPX4 water resistance, and heart rate monitoring. Read our review.

    In a recent development, the big difference between the Superstrike and other gaming mice lies beneath its main two mouse buttons. It uses haptic actuators instead of mechanical switches, allowing for lower latency and more longevity.

    Industry observers note that A great first portable music player/speaker for kids. It uses insertable NFC cards (sold separately) to play music and stories to keep kiddos occupied and entertained without zoning out in front of the TV. This model supports Bluetooth and 3.5mm for private listening, too.

    Sources indicate that the Nex Playground’s motion-controlled gameplay is designed for ages five and up. It comes with games like Fruit Ninja and Whack-a-Mole Deluxe, but many more titles are available via a subscription. It’s a ton of fun for kids. This is the lowest price so far in 2026. Read our review.

    Nothing has changed in terms of aesthetics, but the Max 2 deliver better sound and some new features. Not exactly worth upgrading for, but fantastic for those who are considering them now. Read our full review.

    It’s hard to find a cooler lamp than Govee’s Uplighter floor lamp at this price. It can light a room, and display a mesmerizing pattern up your wall and onto your ceiling.

    Industry observers note that the Meta Quest 3S is a battery-powered standalone VR headset that has the same chipset as the pricier Quest 3, but with the same lenses and screen resolution as the Quest 2. In addition to being able to play many games from the Meta Store, it can also be connected to a gaming PC to play VR games like Half-Life Alyx. Read our review.

    Industry observers note that sucker Punch’s follow-up to Ghost of Tsushima is everything you could want in a sequel. The open-world revenge epic brims with fluid combat and a host of welcome narrative twists, all set against the gorgeous backdrop of Japan’s Edo period. It’s precisely the type of game photo modes were made for, even if you never use them.

    Recent findings suggest that the Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.

    In a recent development, donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. Its destructible environment allows you to smash your way through each of its 17 levels, and the paths you make will remain intact unless you specifically choose to reset the world. Your companion Paulene’s singing allows you to transform into animals that have abilities that allow you to reach previously inaccessible parts of levels. Read our review.

    Sources indicate that arguably the best thing to come out of The Book of Boba Fett was the Mandalorian’s N-1 Starfighter, which Lego has recreated here in miniature. It’s not quite as impressive as the 1,802-piece version, but the cheaper set still packs plenty of detail, including a spring-loaded shooter.

    According to recent reports, nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive is the best way to relive what is arguably the best Zelda game of all time. The revamped visuals look gorgeous, and while the game’s improved controls might annoy some purists who still cling to the heyday of ’98, we reckon most folks won’t bat an eye.

    A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options. It’s a frame that features Alexa, and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.

    This innovative upcoming smart lock uses the U1 ultra-wideband (UWB) chip in many iPhones and Apple Watches to automatically unlock your door as you approach. It will also work with the new Aliro standard and be compatible with Android phones for hands-free unlocking.

    Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.

    In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.

    Recent findings suggest that control Resonant is all about manipulation — of gravity, not people. Remedy’s excellent sequel to Control is an exhilarating action game, with ever-changing combat, twisted level design, and the weirdest traversal mechanics we’ve seen in a long time.

    Recent findings suggest that the Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage.

    Birdbuddy’s charming, camera-equipped feeder identifies and snaps shots of each bird that stops by, supplementing its 5-megapixel stills with insightful facts via an app. The solar roof helps keep the camera’s battery topped up even when it’s cloudy outside.

    Recent findings suggest that azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.

    Sources indicate that magna-Tiles are a quintessential kids’ toy. The colorful, semi-translucent geometric shapes are a favorite here at The Verge, especially for those of us who prefer the simplicity of building with magnets rather than bricks.

    Lego’s 709-piece kit lets you construct three brick-ified bonsai trees, including a black pine, a ginkgo with yellow leaves, and a wisteria with hanging lilac flowers. It also comes with three ornamental displays, just in case you want a raised stand on which to showcase them.

    The Beam isn’t as powerful as the Sonos Arc, nor can it match the flagship soundbar’s Dolby Atmos immersion bubble. But you still get room-filling surround sound for less money — and the Beam ties into the Sonos ecosystem for added convenience. Read our review.

    Google wants to sell you on the Pro’s software features, but it’s the underlying hardware that makes it a stellar Android handset. The build quality is incredible, the larger telephoto sensor is an improvement, and it now supports faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W wireless charging. Read our review.

    Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design.

    Recent findings suggest that the Insta360 Link 2 offers the same auto-swiveling design as its excellent predecessor, only in a smaller form factor. It also offers a slate of new features, including group tracking and no-follow zones.

    Industry observers note that with 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.

    The Fanttik X9 Pro can inflate a car tire in under a minute, making routine maintenance fast and easy. There are four one-click presets for cars, motorcycles, bikes, and balls, along with a manual mode that reaches a maximum pressure of 150 PSI.

    Sources indicate that these smart lights have beautiful colors, a nice selection of festive scenes, and an easy-to-use app. They are super reliable when paired with a Hue Bridge and also work over Bluetooth. They come in three lengths, work with all the major smart home platforms, and are Matter-compatible.

    Recent findings suggest that the Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.

    No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.

    According to recent reports, the Echo Dot Max features a flat design and a redesigned sound system, which delivers nearly three times the bass as its predecessor. It also offers improved conversation detection and better noise filtering, thanks to Amazon’s fresh AZ3 chip. Read our review.

    It has been revealed that glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.

    Vantage isn’t your typical open-world exploration game. It’s a sci-fi roguelike that has you traversing an alien planet alongside up to five players, each of whom must solve puzzles and complete their mission before their time, morale, or health runs out. It’s not as charming as Stonemaier’s award-winning Wingspan, but it is far more interesting.

    In a recent development, LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they fit seamlessly into any major smart home platform. Best of all, the smart features come at a price that makes buying multipacks more affordable than other brands.

    A quiet, battery-powered fan that moves a lot of air despite its small size, the Switchbot Standing Circulator is a surprisingly versatile smart home addition.

    The last-gen JBL Go 4 has been around for a bit, but the pocket-sized Bluetooth speaker still delivers with up to seven hours of runtime, dual-device connectivity, and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance. You can also pair it with other Go 4 speakers for bigger stereo sound, if desired.

    Sources indicate that fairphone’s latest is a very light update to the 6, adding a newer processor and carrying forward its repairability and ethical values. Tradeoffs compared to a traditional smartphone are few, and the benefits are real.

    The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). It also supports 480Mbps data transfer speeds and, unlike similar power meter-equipped cables, lets you turn off the screen when needed.

    The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.

    Nintendo’s latest Pokémon spinoff for the Switch 2 is part Pokémon, part Minecraft, and part Animal Crossing. Yet, despite borrowing gameplay mechanics from each, the cozy life sim is more than the sum of its expansive, building-centric parts. It’s breezy and warm-hearted, with enough secrets to keep mother dearest occupied for hours on end.

    Google’s newly introduced Pixel 10A introduces faster wired charging, Satellite SOS, and new AI tools like Camera Coach and Auto Best Take. Otherwise, it’s basically the Pixel 9A, with the same Tensor G4 chip and a dual-camera system. Read our review.

    Recent findings suggest that the entry-point into RTX Spark laptops, the Asus ProArt is a creator-focused MacBook Pro wannabe with a sleek blacked-out design and lovely OLED display. Read our initial Nvidia RTX Spark hands-on.

    Revision, November 27th: Updated to include several fresh picks, including those for the Google Pixel 10A and the Acer Switch Air 14.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the manufacturer’s management and governance practices.

    Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P remarked in a statement.

    The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

    According to recent reports, although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

    In August, Nvidia announced prepares to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.

    A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.
